To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

PDSs are not a single, uniform entity but a diverse group of partnerships that vary in the number and type of school sites, the type of educational preparation program, and in the degree of collaboration among the partners.
In summary, our research is concerned with

(1) the selection of sites for the development of nontraditional PDS partnerships, (2) the nature and quality of those partnerships, and (3) the implications of these nontraditional PDS sites and partnerships for educational reform and restructuring.

the PDS movement has not lived up to its promise of reforming schools and teacher education programs.
nontraditional PDS sites, atypical collaboration, and the responsibility and role of SCDEs in selecting and developing nontraditional PDS are important and should be encouraged.

nontraditional PDS sites, atypical partnerships, and the responsibility that schools, colleges, or departments of education have for selecting and developing them are important to the future of educational reform and restructuring.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we are trying to understand what it is that PDSs do and what they are likely to do in the future, and what it will take for them to have a significant impact on the education of teachers and on the reform of schools.

we are trying to develop and implement a model of a PDS that is based on a partnership between a SCDE and a school district, that is focused on the preparation of educators, that is located in a school district that is undergoing reform, and that is located in an urban setting with a large percentage of minority students.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the traditional model of PDSs, which are based at one site, is not necessarily the best or only way to implement PDSs.

the traditional PDS model, as defined and described in the Holmes Group reports and other documents (Holmes Group Report, 1990, 1995; National Council for Accreditation of Teacher Education, 1997), is too limiting.
PDSs can and should be more broadly conceived than the typical PDS model that is currently being implemented.
